newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Stals sees small increase in Q4 '96 GDP.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Stals sees small increase in Q4 '96 GDP.

text.p: South African Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Thursday he expected a small increase in gross domestic product growth in the fourth quarter of 1996, helped by an export-led recovery in the manufacturing sector.
"There has been a slight recovery in the fourth quarter, particularly in the manufacturing sector," Stals told a roadshow of market participants.
While national accounts were not yet available, Stals said Reserve Bank estimates suggested there had been a small increase in the quarterly growth rate in the period.
At the same time, real gross domestic expenditure appeared to be stabilising and a small decline was possible in the fourth quarter, Stals said.
"We are moving to a situation where real gross domestic expenditure is moving at around the same level as gross domestic product," he said.

Stals said there were encouraging signs that exporters were already benefitting from the depreciation of the rand in 1996 and commentators should be careful about being too pessimistic about growth prospects in 1997.

Stals said the current account of the balance of payments was improving strongly, boosting South Africa's reserves, which he estimated had risen by some 3.5 billion rand in the fourth quarter of 1996.
However, this had not been fully reflected in the Reserve Bank's own reserves figures since some had gone to commercial banks.
Stals said he was optimistic that South Africa would manage to cap M3 money supply growth at 10 percent in 1997, but stressed that inflation remained a major threat.
"Inflation is where the big problem will be in monetary policy in 1997," he said.
There was an inevitable time lag in the effects of the 22-23 percent fall in the rand in 1996 feeding through to prices, he said.

The challenge for monetary authorities was to prevent an escalation in inflationary expectations, particularly in the labour market. He noted that unit labour costs had been increasing during 1996, reversing the encouraging trend of the previous year.

However, Stals said he was hopeful that inflation would come down again in the second half of 1997, but for the time being the central bank would continue to focus on bearing down on inflation and money supply and credit extension growth via a restrictive monetary policy.
